claim: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a congenital heart disease characterized by underdevelopment of the left ventricle, mitral and aortic valves, and aortic arch.
source: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a congenital heart disease (CHD) characterized by underdevelopment of the left ventricle, mitral and aortic valves, and aortic arch.
evidence: This is a definitional statement from the introduction that establishes the clinical characteristics of HLHS.

claim: Variable phenotypic manifestations and familial inheritance patterns suggest that HLHS is genetically heterogeneous and may have significant environmental contributors.
source: Variable phenotypic manifestations and familial inheritance patterns, together with the numerous studies linking it to a diverse array of genes, suggest that HLHS is genetically heterogeneous and may have significant environmental contributors (Elliott et al., 2003; Iascone et al., 2012; Theis et al., 2015a; Theis et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is based on observed patterns in HLHS cases.

claim: Mice deficient for Sap130 and Pcdha9 exhibited left ventricular hypoplasia likely due to defective cardiomyocyte proliferation and differentiation, and increased cell death.
source: Based on a digenic mechanism, mice deficient for HDAC-associated protein-encoding Sap130 and protocadherin-coding Pcdha9 exhibited left ventricular (LV) hypoplasia that was likely due – at least in part – to defective cardiomyocyte proliferation and differentiation, and increased cell death (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study (Liu et al., 2017) describing an animal model.

claim: HLHS-LV samples have more DNA damage and senescence with cell cycle arrest, and fewer cardiac progenitors and myocytes than controls.
source: Similarly in humans, Gaber et al., 2013 provide evidence that HLHS-LV samples have more DNA damage and senescence with cell cycle arrest, and fewer cardiac progenitors and myocytes than controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published study (Gaber et al., 2013) on human HLHS samples.

claim: Impaired cardiomyocyte proliferation could be a mechanism contributing to HLHS pathogenesis.
source: These observations suggest that impaired cardiomyocyte proliferation could be a mechanism contributing to HLHS pathogenesis, although pathogenic genes controlling this process in humans remain to be identified and validated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations cited in the previous studies.

claim: The male proband (II.3) was diagnosed with non-syndromic HLHS by physical examination and echocardiography.
source: The male proband (II.3) was diagnosed with non-syndromic HLHS by physical examination and echocardiography, which demonstrated aortic and mitral valve atresia, virtual absence of the left ventricular cavity, and severe aortic arch hypoplasia.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the study's patient cohort.

claim: The proband was born prematurely at 29 weeks gestation.
source: He was born prematurely at 29 weeks gestation and underwent staged surgical palliation at 2 and 11 months of age.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient's medical history.

claim: The proband underwent staged surgical palliation at 2 and 11 months of age.
source: He was born prematurely at 29 weeks gestation and underwent staged surgical palliation at 2 and 11 months of age.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient's medical history.

claim: Conversion to a fenestrated Fontan circulation at 3 years of age failed owing to systolic and diastolic heart failure.
source: Conversion to a fenestrated Fontan circulation at 3 years of age failed owing to systolic and diastolic heart failure, necessitating early take-down.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient's medical history.

claim: The patient subsequently died of multi-organ system failure.
source: The patient subsequently died of multi-organ system failure.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient's medical history.

claim: Echocardiography revealed structurally and functionally normal hearts in the proband's mother, father and siblings.
source: Echocardiography revealed structurally and functionally normal hearts in the proband's mother (I.2), father (I.1) and siblings (II.1 and II.2).
evidence: This is clinical data from echocardiographic examination of family members.

claim: Maternal history is notable for four miscarriages.
source: Maternal history is notable for four miscarriages.
evidence: This is clinical data from the maternal medical history.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis revealed 5104 differentially expressed transcripts in d25 differentiated samples between proband vs. mother/father.
source: In this in vitro cellular context, bioinformatic analysis revealed 5104 differentially expressed transcripts (DETs) in d25 differentiated samples between proband vs. mother/father (Supplementary file 1, Benjamini-corrected p<0.001).
evidence: This is data from RNA sequencing analysis of patient-derived iPSCs.

claim: 1,401 differentially expressed transcripts were concordantly differentially expressed between proband and both parents.
source: We found that 1,401 DETs were concordantly differentially expressed between proband and both parents (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 1, 2).
evidence: This is data from RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 1C and supplementary files.

claim: KEGG analysis revealed TP53 pathway enrichment in proband cells.
source: Consistent with previous observations in HLHS fetuses (Gaber et al., 2013), KEGG analysis revealed TP53 pathway enrichment (Figure 1D), including cell cycle inhibition (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with cell proliferation being affected in proband cells.
evidence: This is data from KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Proband hiPSC-CMs exhibited reduced percentage of EdU-positive cells as compared to parents.
source: Indeed, proband hiPSC-CMs exhibited reduced percentage of EdU-positive cells as compared to parents (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is experimental data from EdU-incorporation assays shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claim: The proband cells of families 75H and 151H exhibited significant reduction of proliferative activity as compared to the parents.
source: Consistent with our findings with 5H family-trio cells (Figure 1G,H), the proband cells of families 75H and 151H also exhibited significant reduction of proliferative activity as compared to the parents using the EdU-incorporation assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from EdU-incorporation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of TP53 and CDKN1A in proband hiPSC-CMs significantly increased EdU incorporation as compared to siControl.
source: Indeed, siRNA-mediated knockdown (KD) of TP53 and CDKN1A in proband hiPSC-CMs significantly increased EdU incorporation as compared to siControl (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1I and 1J.

claim: Array comparative genome hybridization ruled out a chromosomal deletion or duplication in the proband.
source: Array comparative genome hybridization ruled out a chromosomal deletion or duplication in the proband.
evidence: This is data from comparative genome hybridization analysis.

claim: WGS was performed on genomic DNA samples from all five family members, based on 101 base paired-end reads that passed quality control standards.
source: WGS was carried out on genomic DNA samples from all five family members, based on 101 base paired-end reads that passed quality control standards; 92% of the reads mapped to the genome.
evidence: This is methodological data from whole-genome sequencing.

claim: 92% of the reads mapped to the genome.
source: WGS was carried out on genomic DNA samples from all five family members, based on 101 base paired-end reads that passed quality control standards; 92% of the reads mapped to the genome.
evidence: This is data from whole-genome sequencing analysis.

claim: Over 99% of the hg19 human reference genome had coverage.
source: After marking and filtering out duplicate reads, over 99% of the hg19 human reference genome had coverage.
evidence: This is data from whole-genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The average depth across the genome was 36X.
source: The average depth across the genome was 36X and an average of 91% of the gene body regions (exons, introns, and 5' and 3' untranslated regions) demonstrated a minimal read depth of 20 reads.
evidence: This is data from whole-genome sequencing analysis.

claim: An average of 91% of the gene body regions demonstrated a minimal read depth of 20 reads.
source: The average depth across the genome was 36X and an average of 91% of the gene body regions (exons, introns, and 5' and 3' untranslated regions) demonstrated a minimal read depth of 20 reads.
evidence: This is data from whole-genome sequencing analysis.

claim: WGS of the family quintet was filtered for rare de novo, recessive and loss-of-function variants with predicted impact on protein structure or expression, yielding 114 variants in 61 genes.
source: To identify novel HLHS candidate genes, WGS of the family quintet was filtered for rare de novo, recessive and loss-of-function variants with predicted impact on protein structure or expression, yielding 114 variants in 61 genes (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1,, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is data from bioinformatic filtering of WGS data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary files.

claim: Ten genes harboring compound heterozygous, hemizygous, or homozygous recessive variants were found to be differentially expressed within the HLHS proband's iPSCs at d0 and d25: HSPG2, APOB, LRP2, PRTG, SLC9A1, SDHD, JPT1, ELF4, HS6ST2, and SIK1.
source: Ten genes harboring compound heterozygous (7), hemizygous (2), or homozygous (1) recessive variants (Table 1), absent in the unaffected siblings, were found to be differentially expressed within the HLHS proband's iPSCs at d0 and d25: HSPG2, APOB, LRP2, PRTG, SLC9A1, SDHD, JPT1, ELF4, HS6ST2, and SIK1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from integrated WGS and RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: qPCR confirmed reduced expression of these genes in proband in d25 iPSC-CM, compared to the parental cells.
source: qPCR confirmed reduced expression of these genes in proband in d25 iPSC-CM, compared to the parental cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from qPCR validation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fly hearts heterozygous for LRP2/mgl show increased end-diastolic diameters.
source: Example of fly hearts heterozygous for LRP2/mgl show increased end-diastolic diameters (EDD, measured at green line in D). Wilcoxon rank sum test: ***p<0.001.
evidence: This is experimental data from Drosophila heart analysis shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: KD of APOB or LRP2 reduced EdU incorporation in hiPSC-CM.
source: KD of APOB (red bar) or LRP2 (green bar) reduced EdU incorporation. **p<0.01 one-way ANOVA.
evidence: This is experimental data from EdU-incorporation assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: TP53 and CDKN1A are upregulated in hiPSC-CM upon KD of APOB or LRP2.
source: qPCR results of TP53 and CDKN1A in hiPSC-CM upon KD of APOB or LRP2. *p<0.05 one-way ANOVA.
evidence: This is experimental data from qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Heart-specific KD of LRP2 (mgl) and JPT1 (CG1943) caused dilated heart phenotypes in Drosophila.
source: By in vivo heart structure and function analysis (Fink et al., 2009; Ocorr et al., 2014), we found that KD of LRP2 (mgl) and JPT1 (CG1943) caused dilated heart phenotypes, while KD of APOB (apolpp), a circulating lipoprotein ligand, and again LRP2 (mgl), resulted in arrhythmias (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Videos 1–3), suggesting developmental defects of cardiac structure and function.
evidence: This is experimental data from Drosophila heart analysis shown in Figure 2B-D and supplementary figures.

claim: KD of APOB (apolpp) and LRP2 (mgl) resulted in arrhythmias in Drosophila.
source: By in vivo heart structure and function analysis (Fink et al., 2009; Ocorr et al., 2014), we found that KD of LRP2 (mgl) and JPT1 (CG1943) caused dilated heart phenotypes, while KD of APOB (apolpp), a circulating lipoprotein ligand, and again LRP2 (mgl), resulted in arrhythmias (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Videos 1–3), suggesting developmental defects of cardiac structure and function.
evidence: This is experimental data from Drosophila heart analysis shown in Figure 2B-D and supplementary figures.

claim: Heart-specific KD of HSPG2/Perlecan (trol) and SDHD (SdhD) exhibited a constricted phenotype in the heterozygous background for tinman/NKX2-5.
source: In this in vivo context, heart-specific KD of two out of nine genes, HSPG2/Perlecan (trol), involved in extracellular matrix assembly (Sasse et al., 2008), and Succinate dehydrogenase subunit D SDHD (SdhD) exhibited a constricted phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 3G,H).
evidence: This is experimental data from Drosophila heart analysis in a sensitized genetic background shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: LRP2 and APOB caused a marked reduction of EdU+ hiPSC-CMs (ACTN1+) and overall hiPSC cell numbers.
source: Remarkably, two of the genes causing cardiac abnormalities when knocked down in Drosophila (Figure 2B–D), LRP2 and APOB, also caused a marked reduction of EdU+ hiPSC-CMs (ACTN1+) and overall hiPSC cell numbers (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data from EdU-incorporation assays shown in Figure 2E, 2F and supplementary figures.

claim: An upregulation of cell cycle inhibitors and apoptosis genes was observed upon LRP2 and APOB knockdown.
source: Notably, we also observed an upregulation of cell cycle inhibitors and apoptosis genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), including TP53 and CDKN1A (Figure 2G), as well as a downregulation of cell cycle genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B,C).
evidence: This is experimental data from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2G and supplementary figures.

claim: HLHS patients had a ~3 fold increase in the frequency of rare, predicted-damaging LRP2 missense variants compared to healthy controls (10% versus 3.4%; p=0.0008).
source: Remarkably, HLHS patients had a ~ 3 fold increase in the frequency of rare, predicted-damaging LRP2 missense variants compared to healthy controls (10% versus 3.4%; p=0.0008) (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is data from rare variant burden analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplementary files.

claim: Among the 13 patients who carried a LRP2 variant, three shared the same predicted-damaging variant (N3205D) with the 5H proband.
source: Among the 13 patients who carried a LRP2 variant (Figure 3A,B), three shared the same predicted-damaging variant (N3205D) with the 5H proband (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is data from variant analysis shown in Figure 3A, 3B and supplementary files.

claim: LRP2 mRNA levels were lower in the probands of both 5H and 49H families, as well as in the parent carrying the variant, compared to non-variant carrying parent.
source: Interestingly, qPCR results showed that LRP2 mRNA levels were lower in the probands of both families, as well as in the parent carrying the variant (CP), compared to non-variant carrying parent (NCP) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is experimental data from qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Hearts from zebrafish larvae with reduced lrp2a function displayed a hypoplastic phenotype with decreased CM number.
source: Hearts from larvae with reduced lrp2a function displayed a hypoplastic phenotype with decreased CM number (Figure 3E–G) and dose-dependent reductions in ventricular chamber dimensions in morphants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is experimental data from zebrafish heart analysis shown in Figure 3E-G and supplementary figures.

claim: Loss-of-lrp2a-function compromised ventricular contractility and caused bradycardia in both morphants and CRISPR-edited larvae.
source: Loss-of-lrp2a-function also compromised ventricular contractility and caused bradycardia in both morphants and CRISPR-edited larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is experimental data from zebrafish heart analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and 1G.

claim: All five validated candidate genes (APOB, HS6ST2, HSPG2, JPT1, LRP2) were connected to WNT and SHH signaling cascades.
source: Strikingly, in addition to TP53 pathway misregulation (Figure 1D–E, Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), all five genes were connected to WNT and SHH signaling cascades, both key regulators of cardiac differentiation and proliferation (Briggs et al., 2016; Gessert and Kühl, 2010; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is data from gene network analysis shown in Figure 4A, supported by citations.

claim: The negative regulator of SHH pathway, PTCH1, was upregulated in proband cells compared to parental cells.
source: Interestingly, RNA-seq analysis of the proband cells is consistent with this network prediction: the negative regulator of SHH pathway, PTCH1, was upregulated, while agonists of WNT signaling pathway, WNT1/3a/8a/10b and FZD10 (Dawson et al., 2013), were downregulated, compared to parental cells.
evidence: This is data from RNA-seq analysis of proband cells.

claim: Agonists of WNT signaling pathway, WNT1/3a/8a/10b and FZD10, were downregulated in proband cells compared to parental cells.
source: Interestingly, RNA-seq analysis of the proband cells is consistent with this network prediction: the negative regulator of SHH pathway, PTCH1, was upregulated, while agonists of WNT signaling pathway, WNT1/3a/8a/10b and FZD10 (Dawson et al., 2013), were downregulated, compared to parental cells.
evidence: This is data from RNA-seq analysis of proband cells.

claim: KD of LRP2 led to reduced FZD10 and increased PTCH1 RNA levels in healthy control hiPSC-CM.
source: Indeed, KD of LRP2 led to reduced FZD10 and increased PTCH1 RNA levels (Figure 4B,C), although WNT1/3a/8/10a were not affected.
evidence: This is experimental data from qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: LRP2 KD significantly reduced both BIO- and siPTCH1-induced proliferation in hiPSC-CMs.
source: We found that LRP2 KD significantly reduced both BIO- and siPTCH1-induced proliferation in hiPSC-CMs (Figure 4D–G), suggesting that LRP2 is required for both WNT- and SHH-regulated CM proliferation.
evidence: This is experimental data from EdU-incorporation assays shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: LRP2 is required for both WNT- and SHH-regulated CM proliferation.
source: We found that LRP2 KD significantly reduced both BIO- and siPTCH1-induced proliferation in hiPSC-CMs (Figure 4D–G), suggesting that LRP2 is required for both WNT- and SHH-regulated CM proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claim: Mutations in LRP2 have been previously associated with left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) as well as other congenital heart defects in mouse.
source: Mutations in LRP2 have been previously associated with left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) as well as other congenital heart defects in mouse (Baardman et al., 2016) and in Donnai-Barrow Syndrome in humans (Baardman et al., 2016; Kantarci et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in LRP2 have been associated with Donnai-Barrow Syndrome in humans.
source: Mutations in LRP2 have been previously associated with left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC) as well as other congenital heart defects in mouse (Baardman et al., 2016) and in Donnai-Barrow Syndrome in humans (Baardman et al., 2016; Kantarci et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LRP2 has not previously been linked to HLHS within curated bioinformatic networks.
source: However, LRP2 has not previously been linked to HLHS within curated bioinformatic networks.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior evidence in bioinformatic databases.

claim: The fundamental mechanisms of heart development and function are remarkably conserved between Drosophila and vertebrates, including a common transcriptional regulatory network.
source: Although overall heart structure in flies differs from that in vertebrates, the fundamental mechanisms of heart development and function are remarkably conserved, including a common transcriptional regulatory network (Bodmer, 1995; Cripps and Olson, 2002), a shared protein composition (Cammarato et al., 2011), as well as electrical and metabolic properties (Ocorr et al., 2014; Ocorr et al., 2007; Diop and Bodmer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Rare, predicted-damaging LRP2 variants were enriched in a HLHS cohort.
source: Interestingly, rare, predicted-damaging LRP2 variants were enriched in a HLHS cohort; however, understanding their contribution to HLHS requires further investigation.
evidence: This is data from rare variant burden analysis in the HLHS cohort.

claim: Compared to parents, the proband's iPSC-CMs exhibited reduced proliferation.
source: Consistent with hypoplastic heart defects, compared to parents the proband's iPSC-CMs exhibited reduced proliferation.
evidence: This is experimental data from EdU-incorporation assays.

claim: LRP2 is required for cardiomyocyte proliferation and differentiation.
source: siRNA/RNAi-mediated knockdown in healthy human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CM) and in developing Drosophila and zebrafish hearts revealed that LDL receptor-related protein LRP2 is required for cardiomyocyte proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data across multiple model systems.

claim: Drosophila has been established as an efficient model system to identify key genes and mechanisms critical for heart development and function that served as prototypes for vertebrate/mammalian studies.
source: Drosophila has been established as an efficient model system to identify key genes and mechanisms critical for heart development and function that served as prototypes for vertebrate/mammalian studies, including in zebrafish and mice, due to high degree of conservation of genetic pathways and reduced genetic complexity (Bodmer and Frasch, 2010), e.g. the first cardiogenic transcription factor Nkx2-5/tinman, discovered in Drosophila (Azpiazu and Frasch, 1993; Bodmer, 1993), marked the beginning of a molecular-genetic understanding of cardiac specification (Bodmer, 1995; Cripps and Olson, 2002; Benson et al., 1999; Cordes and Srivastava, 2009; Qian and Srivastava, 2013; Kathiriya et al., 2015; Fahed et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The first cardiogenic transcription factor Nkx2-5/tinman was discovered in Drosophila.
source: Drosophila has been established as an efficient model system to identify key genes and mechanisms critical for heart development and function that served as prototypes for vertebrate/mammalian studies, including in zebrafish and mice, due to high degree of conservation of genetic pathways and reduced genetic complexity (Bodmer and Frasch, 2010), e.g. the first cardiogenic transcription factor Nkx2-5/tinman, discovered in Drosophila (Azpiazu and Frasch, 1993; Bodmer, 1993), marked the beginning of a molecular-genetic understanding of cardiac specification (Bodmer, 1995; Cripps and Olson, 2002; Benson et al., 1999; Cordes and Srivastava, 2009; Qian and Srivastava, 2013; Kathiriya et al., 2015; Fahed et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The discovery of Nkx2-5/tinman marked the beginning of a molecular-genetic understanding of cardiac specification.
source: Drosophila has been established as an efficient model system to identify key genes and mechanisms critical for heart development and function that served as prototypes for vertebrate/mammalian studies, including in zebrafish and mice, due to high degree of conservation of genetic pathways and reduced genetic complexity (Bodmer and Frasch, 2010), e.g. the first cardiogenic transcription factor Nkx2-5/tinman, discovered in Drosophila (Azpiazu and Frasch, 1993; Bodmer, 1993), marked the beginning of a molecular-genetic understanding of cardiac specification (Bodmer, 1995; Cripps and Olson, 2002; Benson et al., 1999; Cordes and Srivastava, 2009; Qian and Srivastava, 2013; Kathiriya et al., 2015; Fahed et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The digenic mouse HLHS model for Sap130 and pcdha9 has a penetrance of less than 30%.
source: Interestingly, the only mouse HLHS model to date, a digenic mutant for Sap130 and pcdha9 (Liu et al., 2017), has a penetrance of less than 30%, indicating a profound role for subtle differences between genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Liu et al., 2017).

claim: The low penetrance of the Sap130/pcdha9 mouse model indicates a profound role for subtle differences between genetic backgrounds.
source: Interestingly, the only mouse HLHS model to date, a digenic mutant for Sap130 and pcdha9 (Liu et al., 2017), has a penetrance of less than 30%, indicating a profound role for subtle differences between genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of low penetrance in the mouse model.

claim: WNT and SHH signaling cascades are key regulators of cardiac differentiation and proliferation.
source: Strikingly, in addition to TP53 pathway misregulation (Figure 1D–E, Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4), all five genes were connected to WNT and SHH signaling cascades, both key regulators of cardiac differentiation and proliferation (Briggs et al., 2016; Gessert and Kühl, 2010; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LVNC is often accompanied by other CHDs.
source: In fact, LVNC is often accompanied by other CHDs (Stähli et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CHDs in general and HLHS in particular are likely oligogenic and share many common factors.
source: This may again be due to the fact that CHDs in general and HLHS in particular are likely oligogenic and share many common factors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed patterns in CHD genetics.

claim: Approximately 80% of disease-causing human genes have fly orthologs.
source: Not all human genes are conserved in Drosophila, but ~ 80% of disease-causing human genes have fly orthologs.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about gene conservation.

claim: Impaired ventricular growth could be caused by changes in the p53 pathway.
source: Impaired ventricular growth could in addition be caused by changes in the p53 pathway, and our analysis of iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes suggests that p53 indeed depends on LRP2 levels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by experimental data from iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes.

claim: A multi-hit model of HLHS caused by sub-threshold hypomorphic alleles represents an attractive explanation of many CHDs.
source: Such a multi-hit model of HLHS caused by sub-threshold hypomorphic alleles represents an attractive explanation of many CHDs.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the genetic architecture of HLHS.
